items.rationale: A known asthmatic with a 3-day viral trigger, a red-zone peak flow, a silent chest, and worsening hypoxemia is in a severe exacerbation heading toward respiratory failure. Continuous nebulized albuterol with ipratropium reverses bronchospasm fastest, and a systemic corticosteroid started early shortens the attack and prevents rebound, so it is not delayed. Air entry, work of breathing, and oxygen saturation show within minutes whether airflow is returning. Antihistamines do not relieve bronchospasm, oxygen is never withheld from a hypoxemic child, and forced peak flow maneuvers exhaust a child in distress.

items.update: 1455: The charge nurse brings the emergency asthma protocol orders: oxygen titrated to keep SpO2 at 92% or greater, continuous nebulized albuterol with ipratropium bromide, and IV methylprednisolone 2 mg/kg. The child remains drowsy with a silent chest.
items.stem: Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Sit the child fully upright and increase the oxygen to a nonrebreather mask to keep the saturation at 92% or greater.
Administer the ordered IV methylprednisolone.
Begin the continuous nebulized albuterol with ipratropium bromide.
Activate the rapid response team and notify the provider of the silent chest and rising respiratory rate.
Reassess breath sounds, work of breathing, and oxygen saturation 15 minutes after the treatment is started.
items.rationale: Hypoxemia kills first, so the child is positioned upright and the oxygen is escalated before anything else; the continuous bronchodilator follows because it is the only ordered therapy that reopens the airways within minutes. The team is then summoned, since a drowsy child with a silent chest may need intubation and a higher level of care. The corticosteroid is given next because its benefit appears over hours rather than minutes, and a structured reassessment 15 minutes into the treatment tells the nurse whether the plan is working.

items.update: Hospital day 2, 1000: After continuous nebulization, IV corticosteroid, and overnight observation the respirations are 22/min with no retractions, breath sounds are clear with good air entry throughout, SpO2 is 97% on room air, and the peak flow is 240 L/min (86% of personal best). The child is being discharged with a written asthma action plan, a spacer, and a fluticasone refill.
items.stem: The nurse reviews the discharge teaching with the caregiver. For each statement, indicate whether it demonstrates understanding or requires further teaching.
matrixRows: "When his peak flow is between 140 and 220 L/min we are in the yellow zone, so I give the rescue inhaler and call the clinic."
"I will put one puff into the spacer at a time and have him take a slow deep breath in and hold it for about 10 seconds."
"Now that he is better we can stop the fluticasone and just use the rescue inhaler whenever he wheezes."
"The kitten will stay out of his bedroom and I will wash his bedding in hot water every week."
"If his peak flow drops below 140 L/min and the rescue inhaler does not help, I will give another dose in the morning and see how he does."
"He should rinse his mouth and spit after each dose of the fluticasone."
"Spraying the albuterol straight into his mouth without the spacer gets the medicine there faster."
items.rationale: The yellow zone is 50% to 79% of the 280 L/min personal best, so 140 to 220 L/min correctly triggers rescue therapy and a call, while anything below 140 L/min is the red zone and means emergency care now, not a wait until morning. A daily inhaled corticosteroid controls the underlying inflammation and is continued when the child feels well; rinsing and spitting afterward prevents oral candidiasis. Reducing cat dander and dust mite exposure is sound trigger control. A spacer must deliver one puff at a time with a slow deep breath and a 10-second hold, and skipping the spacer deposits most of the dose in the mouth rather than the lungs.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the 0715 handoff note that require the nurse's immediate follow-up.

highlightSegments.text: 0715 handoff: 12-year-old with hemoglobin SS disease, hospital day 1 of a vaso-occlusive pain crisis.
Rates the pain 9 out of 10 in both thighs, the lower back, and the left upper arm, unchanged since admission.
Analgesia is ordered as needed only, and the dose that came due at 0645 has not been given.
Was laughing with a visitor and using a phone at 0500.
Temperature rose to 38.0 C (100.4 F) at 0600.
Heart rate 118/min and blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg.
Oxygen saturation 95% on room air, down from a documented baseline of 98%.
Splinting the chest and taking shallow breaths, and refused to cough and deep breathe because it hurts.
Intravenous fluids are infusing at the ordered maintenance rate.
Scleral icterus is present, unchanged from the admission assessment.
The parent is at the bedside and asks to review the pain medicine schedule.

items.rationale: Severe pain that has not moved in 5 hours while analgesia is ordered as needed only and the due dose is late is a failure of the pain plan, and in a child with functional asplenia a new fever is a medical emergency until sepsis is ruled out. A saturation drifting below baseline together with splinting and shallow breathing are the earliest cues of acute chest syndrome. Laughing and using a phone are distraction strategies children in chronic pain use and never disprove a pain report; icterus is chronic hemolysis, and a mildly raised heart rate with a normal blood pressure is expected in a child in pain.

items.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is an expected baseline finding of sickle cell disease, a finding consistent with the vaso-occlusive crisis, or a finding that suggests a different complication requiring urgent evaluation.
matrixRows: Hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL with a reticulocyte count of 12% (baseline hemoglobin 8.0 to 8.5 g/dL)
Scleral icterus with a total bilirubin of 2.8 mg/dL
Deep aching pain in both thighs and the lower back that began after a cold-water swim meet
Temperature 38.0 C (100.4 F)
Oxygen saturation 95% on room air, down from a baseline of 98%
Pain rated 9 of 10 while the heart rate and blood pressure remain near normal
matrixColumns: Expected baseline in sickle cell disease
items.rationale: Chronic hemolysis keeps the hemoglobin near 8 g/dL with a high reticulocyte count and raises the bilirubin enough to yellow the sclerae, so neither is new. Cold exposure and dehydration trigger sickling, and bone pain in the thighs and back is the classic vaso-occlusive picture; a high self-reported score with near-normal vital signs is also typical, because autonomic responses blunt in recurrent pain. Fever in a child with functional asplenia points to infection and needs cultures and empiric antibiotics, and a falling saturation is the first sign of acute chest syndrome, not of ordinary bone pain.

items.topic: Pain Assessment in Sickle Cell Disease
items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A 12-year-old with hemoglobin SS disease rates vaso-occlusive pain 9 of 10 while the heart rate and blood pressure stay near normal. The nurse prioritizes {{1}} as the client's problem, measures it using {{2}}, and watches for {{3}} as the complication most likely to develop next.

options: anxiety related to missing school
worsening chronic anemia that requires immediate transfusion
unrelieved vaso-occlusive pain from sickled cells obstructing the microcirculation
opioid-seeking behavior that the admission is reinforcing
the child's own numeric pain rating
how relaxed the child looks while visitors are present
the heart rate and blood pressure
the number of doses the child has requested
acute chest syndrome
aplastic crisis
hand-foot syndrome
priapism

items.rationale: The priority problem is ischemic pain from sickled cells blocking the microcirculation, and self-report remains the gold standard for measuring it; labeling a child with sickle cell disease as drug-seeking because the vital signs are near normal or because the child appears distracted leads directly to undertreatment. A hemoglobin close to the child's own baseline does not call for transfusion. With fever, chest splinting, and shallow breathing already present, acute chest syndrome is the complication most likely to follow, and it is the leading cause of death in this population.

items.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor to assess progress.
bowtieConditions: Vaso-occlusive pain crisis with a risk for acute chest syndrome
bowtieActions: Give IV fluids at the maintenance rate and encourage warm oral fluids
Apply ice packs to the painful thighs and back
Restrict fluids to prevent pulmonary edema
Request scheduled around-the-clock IV morphine with a breakthrough dose available
Hold all opioids until the child can be evaluated for substance misuse
bowtieParams: Numeric pain rating before and after each dose
items.rationale: Severe symmetric bone pain after cold exposure in hemoglobin SS disease is a vaso-occlusive crisis, and the fever with chest splinting makes acute chest syndrome the looming risk. Severe crisis pain is continuous, so analgesia is scheduled around the clock with breakthrough doses rather than left as needed, and maintenance-rate fluids with warmth reduce sickling; ice causes vasoconstriction and worsens it, and fluid restriction promotes further sickling. Pain scores before and after each dose show whether the regimen works, while the respiratory rate and saturation watch for both opioid-induced depression and developing acute chest syndrome. A reticulocyte count of 12% rules out aplastic crisis.

items.update: Hospital day 2, 0430: The child reports new sharp right-sided chest pain and a dry cough. Temperature is 38.9 C (102.0 F), respirations 32/min, SpO2 88% on room air, and the chest radiograph shows a new right lower lobe infiltrate.
items.stem: Which actions should the nurse take now? Select all that apply.
options: Increase the IV fluids to twice the maintenance rate to thin the secretions
Apply supplemental oxygen titrated to keep the saturation at 95% or greater
Hold the scheduled opioid because the respiratory rate is elevated
Obtain blood cultures and give the ordered empiric antibiotics that cover atypical organisms
Coach the child to use the incentive spirometer every 2 hours while awake
Keep the child on bed rest with the head of the bed flat to conserve energy
Notify the provider of the new infiltrate, the fever, and the hypoxemia
items.rationale: New chest pain, fever, hypoxemia, and an infiltrate in sickle cell disease define acute chest syndrome, which deteriorates quickly: oxygen to a saturation of at least 95% interrupts further sickling, the provider is notified at once, and cultures followed by antibiotics covering atypical organisms treat the common triggers. Incentive spirometry every 2 hours keeps the alveoli open and is the single best bedside measure against progression. The opioid is continued, because pain that makes a child splint causes the hypoventilation that drives the syndrome, and fluid overload floods the lungs, so fluids stay at maintenance and the head of the bed stays elevated.

items.update: Hospital day 4, 0800: The child has completed 48 hours of IV antibiotics, the scheduled IV morphine has been changed to oral oxycodone, and incentive spirometry is being done every 2 hours.
items.stem: The nurse reviews the trended data. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: The falling temperature with rising spirometry volumes indicates the child is becoming oversedated
The child no longer needs oxygen saturation monitoring or incentive spirometry
The acute chest syndrome is resolving and the pain is responding to the current regimen
The opioid should be stopped today because the pain rating has reached 3
items.rationale: Every parameter is moving the right way: defervescence, a respiratory rate returning to the normal 14 to 22 range for a 12-year-old, a saturation back to baseline on room air, and spirometry volumes that have nearly tripled as splinting eases, all alongside pain that has fallen from 9 to 3. Oversedation would slow the respiratory rate below normal and shrink the spirometry volumes, not improve them. Opioids are tapered rather than stopped abruptly while pain persists, and monitoring and spirometry continue until discharge because acute chest syndrome can recur.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the 1015 nursing summary. Click to highlight the findings that require immediate follow-up.

highlightSegments.text: 1015 nursing summary: 78-year-old client admitted this morning after 4 days of vomiting and diarrhea at home.
Blood pressure has improved from 96/58 to 108/64 mm Hg after 1,000 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride.
Urine output totals 62 mL since the catheter was inserted at 0600, with 14 mL in the last hour.
Serum creatinine has risen from a clinic value of 1.0 mg/dL three weeks ago to 3.4 mg/dL this morning.
Temperature 36.9 C (98.4 F) and lungs clear to auscultation.
Serum potassium 6.4 mEq/L on a repeat, non-hemolyzed specimen.
Hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL and hematocrit 44%.
The radial pulse is now irregular, and the client says both legs feel too heavy to lift.
Client is oriented to person, place, and time.
SpO2 98% on room air.
The client's child brought the home medication bottles in for reconciliation.

items.rationale: Urine output of 62 mL in four and a half hours is about 0.2 mL/kg/hr, well below the 0.5 mL/kg/hr threshold for oliguria, and a creatinine that has more than tripled from a recent baseline confirms an acute drop in filtration. A potassium of 6.4 mEq/L verified on a non-hemolyzed sample, with a new irregular pulse and profound leg weakness, is a life-threatening electrolyte emergency. The improving blood pressure, normal temperature, clear lungs, normal hemoglobin and normal oxygen saturation are reassuring findings, not urgent ones.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: The nurse reviews the 0930 results for this 78-year-old client: urine output 62 mL in 4.5 hours, creatinine risen from 1.0 to 3.4 mg/dL with a BUN of 66 mg/dL, urine sodium 12 mEq/L with a fractional excretion of sodium below 1%, urine specific gravity 1.030, and a sediment with no protein, blood or casts. These findings indicate {{1}} acute kidney injury caused mainly by {{2}}. The nurse should interpret the potassium of 6.4 mEq/L as {{3}}.

options: postrenal
intrarenal (intrinsic)
prerenal
direct tubular damage from IV contrast dye
reduced kidney perfusion made worse by the lisinopril and the naproxen
an autoimmune attack on the glomerular basement membrane
obstruction of urine flow below the bladder neck
an expected effect of the 0.9% sodium chloride infusion
a laboratory error caused by a hemolyzed specimen
a true value the failing kidneys can no longer excrete

items.rationale: A BUN-to-creatinine ratio near 20:1, a urine sodium of 12 mEq/L with a fractional excretion of sodium under 1%, concentrated urine and a bland sediment are the classic pattern of prerenal injury: the kidneys are underperfused but still able to conserve sodium and water. Volume loss from four days of vomiting and diarrhea is compounded by an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor, which dilates the efferent arteriole, and a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug, which constricts the afferent arteriole, so glomerular pressure collapses. No contrast was given and the bladder scan was only 50 mL, ruling out tubular and obstructive causes, and the repeat non-hemolyzed sample confirms the potassium is real.

items.update: 1015: The 12-lead ECG shows tall, narrow, peaked T waves in leads V2 through V4 with a PR interval of 0.24 seconds and a QRS of 0.12 seconds. A repeat potassium drawn at 1010 is 6.6 mEq/L.
items.stem: Which hypothesis should the nurse prioritize at this moment?
options: Life-threatening hyperkalemia with a risk of ventricular dysrhythmia and cardiac arrest
Uremic encephalopathy from the rising blood urea nitrogen
Symptomatic hypocalcemia causing the perioral tingling and weakness
Hypovolemic shock from continued gastrointestinal fluid losses
items.rationale: Peaked T waves with a lengthening PR interval and a widening QRS mean the hyperkalemia is already changing cardiac conduction, and the next steps on that path are a sine-wave pattern, ventricular fibrillation and asystole, so this is the hypothesis that drives immediate action. Volume depletion is real but is being corrected and the blood pressure is rising. A BUN of 66 mg/dL can cause lethargy but not sudden death, and the calcium of 8.2 mg/dL is only mildly low and does not explain the ECG changes.

items.update: 1025: The provider is at the bedside writing orders for the acute kidney injury and the hyperkalemia. The client remains on continuous cardiac monitoring.
items.stem: For each prescription, specify whether the nurse should anticipate it or question it for this client at this time.
matrixRows: Hold the lisinopril and the naproxen
Add potassium chloride 20 mEq to each liter of maintenance IV fluid
10% calcium gluconate 10 mL IV over 3 minutes with continuous cardiac monitoring
Ibuprofen 400 mg orally every 6 hours as needed for knee pain
Hold the metformin while the creatinine is elevated
Regular insulin 10 units IV with 50% dextrose 25 g IV
Consult nephrology for possible urgent hemodialysis
items.rationale: Both the angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor and the nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug strip away the kidney's ability to autoregulate perfusion, so they are held, and metformin is held because it accumulates in kidney failure and raises the risk of lactic acidosis. Calcium gluconate stabilizes the myocardium against the hyperkalemia and insulin with dextrose shifts potassium into the cells, while nephrology is consulted early because dialysis is the definitive removal route if the level does not fall. Adding potassium to the fluids or giving another nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug would worsen both problems and must be questioned.

items.update: 1040: The prescriptions for emergency hyperkalemia management are entered and all medications are at the bedside. Place the steps in the correct order.
items.stem: Place the steps in the correct order for the nurse to carry out the emergency management of this client's hyperkalemia.
options: Report the repeat values to the provider and prepare the client for urgent hemodialysis if the potassium remains elevated
Recheck the serum potassium and a point-of-care glucose 30 minutes after the insulin dose
Give regular insulin 10 units IV with 50% dextrose 25 g to shift potassium into the cells
Administer 10% calcium gluconate 10 mL IV over 3 minutes while watching the cardiac monitor
Administer sodium zirconium cyclosilicate 10 g orally to remove potassium from the body
items.rationale: IV calcium is given first because it does nothing to the potassium level but antagonizes its effect at the cardiac membrane within minutes, buying time against a fatal dysrhythmia. Insulin with dextrose follows and drives potassium into the cells in about 15 minutes, a temporary shift, so a gastrointestinal binder is then given to actually remove potassium from the body. Rechecking the potassium and the glucose detects both a rebound and insulin-induced hypoglycemia, and hemodialysis is the definitive treatment when an oliguric client cannot excrete the load.

items.update: Hospital day 4: The client has received isotonic IV fluids, the lisinopril, naproxen and metformin have remained on hold, and dialysis was never required.
items.stem: Which conclusion should the nurse draw from the trended data?
options: The normalizing potassium means the naproxen and the lisinopril can safely be restarted today.
The rising urine output indicates fluid overload, and a loop diuretic should be requested.
The injury has progressed to chronic kidney disease, and long-term dialysis should be arranged.
Kidney function is recovering and the client has entered the diuretic phase, so fluid balance and electrolytes still need close monitoring.
items.rationale: A creatinine falling toward baseline with a potassium back in range and urine output climbing past 2 L a day is the recovery, or diuretic, phase of prerenal acute kidney injury, when the tubules resume flow before they fully resume concentrating, so the client can now lose too much fluid, potassium and sodium. The weight gain reflects rehydration from the isotonic fluids rather than overload, since the client is still below the 72 kg clinic weight. Dialysis is not indicated in a recovering kidney, and the nephrotoxic drugs are restarted only after the creatinine has stabilized and the provider has reviewed alternatives for the knee pain.

items.stem: The nurse assumes care at 0800 and reviews the chart. Which findings require immediate follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: Respiratory rate 10/min and shallow
Flapping tremor of the hands when the wrists are extended
Temperature 37.3 C (99.1 F)
SpO2 97% on 6 L/min by nasal cannula
Hemoglobin 16.4 g/dL with hematocrit 51%
Client's reported usual oxygen saturation at home in the high 80s
Diminished breath sounds with expiratory wheezes documented on admission
Client arouses only to loud voice and then falls back asleep
items.rationale: A fall in level of consciousness is the earliest reliable sign of carbon dioxide retention, and a respiratory rate that has dropped from 28/min to 10/min means the client is no longer blowing off carbon dioxide. Asterixis, the flapping tremor, is a hallmark of hypercapnia, and a saturation of 97% is far above this client's prescribed 88% to 92% target, which points to the oxygen increase as the trigger. The low-grade temperature, the wheezes, a home saturation in the high 80s and a hematocrit of 51% are all expected in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with chronic hypoxemia.

items.update: 0840: The arterial blood gas drawn at 0830 has resulted. The client remains on 6 L/min by nasal cannula.
items.stem: Which conclusion should the nurse draw from the trended data?
options: There is worsening acute respiratory acidosis on top of chronic carbon dioxide retention, and the somnolence is carbon dioxide narcosis.
The rising PaO2 confirms the oxygen therapy is effective, and the slower respiratory rate reflects restful sleep.
The primary problem is a metabolic alkalosis from the IV corticosteroid, and the lungs are compensating for it.
The values show an acute asthma attack, and the falling respiratory rate means the bronchospasm has resolved.
items.rationale: The admission gas shows compensated chronic hypercapnia, a pH of 7.35 with a PaCO2 of 56 mm Hg and a bicarbonate of 30 mEq/L, which is this client's normal. As the PaCO2 climbs to 82 mm Hg the pH falls to 7.25, so the acidosis is now acute and uncompensated, and it tracks exactly with the oxygen increase, the falling respiratory rate and the falling level of consciousness. A high bicarbonate here is chronic renal compensation, not a primary alkalosis, and a PaO2 of 96 mm Hg is not reassurance but a sign of overcorrection: a slowing respiratory rate in a breathless client is deterioration, never rest.

items.update: 0845: The provider is at the bedside. The client arouses only to a firm shoulder squeeze, respirations are 10/min and shallow, and SpO2 is 97% on 6 L/min by nasal cannula.
items.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor to assess progress.
bowtieActions: Titrate the oxygen down to maintain an SpO2 of 88% to 92%
Prepare the client for non-invasive positive pressure ventilation
Position the client flat and allow uninterrupted sleep until the next blood gas
Remove all supplemental oxygen and place the client on room air
Administer the as-needed lorazepam to settle the client's restlessness
bowtieParams: Level of consciousness and ability to protect the airway
Serial arterial blood gas pH and PaCO2
items.rationale: A pH of 7.25 with a PaCO2 of 82 mm Hg, a respiratory rate of 10/min and a client who barely rouses is acute hypercapnic respiratory failure: high-flow oxygen has blunted the hypoxic drive and worsened ventilation-perfusion matching, so carbon dioxide has climbed. The oxygen is titrated down to the 88% to 92% target rather than removed, because abruptly stripping it away causes dangerous hypoxemia, and non-invasive positive pressure ventilation is the treatment that actually clears carbon dioxide. Serial gases and level of consciousness show whether ventilation is improving or whether intubation is needed; a sedative would deepen the hypoventilation, and there are no opioids on this record and no findings of pulmonary edema or pneumothorax.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: The provider and the nurse plan care for this client's acute-on-chronic respiratory failure. The nurse titrates the oxygen to a target saturation of {{1}} and anticipates that {{2}} will be started to lower the carbon dioxide. The nurse also holds {{3}}, because it deepens the hypoventilation that caused the problem.

options: greater than 96%
hourly incentive spirometry
a 100% non-rebreather mask at 15 L/min
chest physiotherapy with postural drainage
non-invasive positive pressure ventilation
the IV methylprednisolone
the as-needed lorazepam
the scheduled albuterol-ipratropium nebulizer

items.rationale: In a client who chronically retains carbon dioxide, the goal is a saturation of 88% to 92%, high enough to protect the tissues and low enough to preserve the respiratory drive and avoid worsening ventilation-perfusion mismatch. Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation is the standard treatment for hypercapnic respiratory failure because the inspiratory pressure augments each breath and washes out carbon dioxide, often avoiding intubation. The bronchodilator and the IV corticosteroid are the backbone of exacerbation treatment and continue, but the as-needed benzodiazepine is held, since sedatives blunt the drive to breathe in an already somnolent client.

items.update: 0905: Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation is prescribed at an inspiratory pressure of 12 cm H2O and an expiratory pressure of 5 cm H2O with an FiO2 of 28%. Respiratory therapy is at the bedside applying the mask.
items.stem: Which action should the nurse take as the non-invasive positive pressure ventilation is started?
options: Darken the room, let the client sleep undisturbed, and recheck in 1 hour
Administer the as-needed lorazepam so that the client tolerates the mask
Raise the head of the bed to at least 30 degrees, confirm the mask seal, and stay with the client to coach breathing and watch for gastric distention
Increase the FiO2 to 60% until the SpO2 is above 95%
items.rationale: Elevating the head of the bed improves diaphragmatic excursion and reduces the aspiration risk created by air forced into the stomach, and a proper seal is what makes the pressure reach the lungs instead of leaking past the mask. Staying with the client during the first minutes is what determines whether non-invasive ventilation succeeds, since most failures are intolerance, and it is also when deterioration toward intubation shows itself. A sedative would worsen the hypoventilation, raising the FiO2 pushes the saturation back above the safe target, and leaving a somnolent hypercapnic client alone risks an unwitnessed respiratory arrest.

items.update: 1100: After 2 hours on non-invasive positive pressure ventilation at an FiO2 of 28%, the repeat arterial blood gas shows pH 7.34, PaCO2 62 mm Hg, HCO3 33 mEq/L, PaO2 68 mm Hg. Respirations 18/min. The client is awake, oriented, and asking for water. The abdomen is distended and tympanic, and the client has not coughed or cleared secretions for the past hour.
items.stem: For each finding, specify whether it indicates that the plan of care has been effective or ineffective.
matrixRows: pH risen from 7.25 to 7.34 with the PaCO2 down from 82 to 62 mm Hg
Abdomen distended and tympanic to percussion
Client awake, oriented, and asking for water
SpO2 90% on an FiO2 of 28%
Respiratory rate 18/min, up from 10/min
No cough or secretion clearance in the past hour
items.rationale: The treatment is working when the carbon dioxide falls, the pH returns toward this client's compensated baseline, the respiratory rate recovers and the level of consciousness clears, and an SpO2 of 90% is exactly the 88% to 92% target, not a value to push higher. A distended, tympanic abdomen is gastric insufflation from the mask pressure, which splints the diaphragm and raises the aspiration risk, so the nurse reports it and anticipates a lower inspiratory pressure or a gastric tube. Retained secretions are the other common reason non-invasive ventilation fails, since the mask blocks effective coughing, and both findings need intervention rather than reassurance.
